outcome: Still open as of 11 Oct 2026. No unconditional progress on the infinitude question since 26 Jan 2024; the only movement bearing on it is a conditional reduction to Schinzel's Hypothesis H in an Erdős-problems forum thread (Feb 2026, with an earlier forum sketch of the same reduction in Aug 2025). No source credits an AI system with anything on balanced primes.
problem_asks: Whether there are infinitely many balanced primes. A balanced prime is a prime p equal to the arithmetic mean of its two neighbouring primes, the previous prime p₋ and the next prime p₊, so that 2p = p₋ + p₊ (OEIS A006562, 'balanced primes of order one'). The statement asks for one thing only: infinitude. It asks for no count, density, growth rate or structure of the set. Equivalently, it asks whether there are infinitely many three-term runs of consecutive primes in arithmetic progression (CPAP-3s), since the middle prime of each CPAP-3 is balanced and every balanced prime is the middle of one.

events.what_happened: Rémi Eismann, 'Decomposition into weight * level + jump and application to a new classification of primes', arXiv:0711.0865. Per a search snippet, the paper restates the balanced-prime question as whether the number of primes of 'level (1;1)' is infinite, and proposes a generalisation to level (1;i) as a conjecture without rigorous argument. I opened only the arXiv abstract page, which does not show that passage, so the restatement rests on the snippet alone. The abstract says the author will 'make a series of conjectures based on numerical data'. The OEIS A006562 entry credits Eismann with a Feb 2007 comment on primes of level (1,k).
events.revisions: v1 6 Nov 2007; v2 1 Jan 2008; v3 14 Jul 2009 (comments say conjecture 9 was added in v3); v4 18 Jan 2010 (version shown on the abstract page).
events.delivers: Nothing that settles the question. Per the snippet it poses the level (1;1) infinitude as a question and offers a conjecture for level (1;i). It proves nothing about infinitude.
events.remains: The whole problem: the infinitude of balanced primes, which the paper poses rather than proves.
events.direction: Neither way. It treats the same quantity as a question and conjectures about a related level, so it leans no way on the answer.

events.what_happened: A finite record, not a result on the question: the largest known CPAP-3 has 15,004 decimal digits and was found by Serge Batalov (Wikipedia 'Balanced prime', as of 2023, citing the primerecords.dk page 'The Largest Known CPAP's', retrieved 2023-01-06). The Wikipedia figure is for the CPAP-3, whose middle prime is the balanced prime. I did not load primerecords.dk; a search summary says the live page could not be loaded.
events.delivers: One finite instance: a single balanced prime of 15,004 digits (as the middle of a CPAP-3). A finite instance of an infinitude claim moves nothing.
events.remains: The whole problem, including the infinitude itself.
events.directly_checkable: The prime can be checked by a primality test; I did not run one.
events.direction: Neither way; it is a single example that is consistent with infinitely many balanced primes but does not bear on whether there are infinitely many.
events.object: A CPAP-3 with 15,004-digit terms, whose middle prime is balanced. Explicit (found by search), not a non-constructive existence result.

events.what_happened: On the OEIS A006562 entry, contributor Alain Rocchelli added two conjectures: on 21 Mar 2024, lim n·(log a(n))²/a(n) = 1/2; and on 23 Mar 2024, the asymptotic of the average of a(n+1) − a(n) is equivalent to 2·(log a(n))², together with 2·Σ(log a(n))² ~ a(N). Both are about how the sequence grows, not whether it is infinite. The entry itself makes no statement on infinitude. Both conjectures are unproven contributor comments.
events.delivers: Nothing. They are conjectures about the growth rate. A limit statement about a(n) presupposes that the sequence is infinite, so they cannot establish infinitude.
events.doubts: They are unproven OEIS contributor conjectures. No proof or discussion of them found.
events.direction: Neither way. Growth-rate conjectures that take infinitude as given.

events.what_happened: Forum post by DesmondWeisenberg on the Erdős Problem #141 thread (erdosproblems.com forum), 16:28 on 11 Aug 2025. Per the fetch summary it discusses the Hardy–Littlewood prime k-tuples conjecture and admissible sets translating into consecutive primes, and does not name Schinzel's Hypothesis H in its claim. Reply by Dogmachine, 16:58 the same day, attributes the underlying reduction to Schinzel and Sierpiński, 'Sur certaines hypothèses concernant les nombres premiers' (1958). I did not check the 1958 paper.
events.delivers: Nothing unconditional. An informal sketch that consecutive-prime progressions follow from admissibility in the prime k-tuples setting, which is itself conjectural.
events.doubts: Informal forum discussion. The sketch relies on the prime k-tuples conjecture, which is open. The attribution to Schinzel–Sierpiński (1958) comes from a reply and is not verified.
events.direction: Conditional and heuristic, leaning affirmative. It proves nothing.

events.what_happened: Forum post by 'Abel' on the Erdős Problem #141 thread, 23:01 on 8 Feb 2026 (forum timestamp). It states a conditional theorem: assuming Schinzel's Hypothesis H (equivalently Dickson's conjecture for linear forms), for every k ≥ 3 there are infinitely many k-term arithmetic progressions of consecutive primes. The k = 3 case is exactly the balanced-prime question, since the middle prime of a CPAP-3 is balanced. The post calls the implication 'generally regarded as folklore' and cites Schinzel–Sierpiński (1958), Dubner et al. (2001) and a MathOverflow discussion. I read it through a fetch summary of the forum page, not verbatim.
events.delivers: Conditional only: if Schinzel's Hypothesis H holds, then there are infinitely many balanced primes (the k = 3 case). Unconditionally, nothing about the infinitude.
events.remains: The unconditional infinitude of balanced primes. Also Schinzel's Hypothesis H, which the argument needs and which is open.
events.doubts: No named expert has verified it. The forum says its comments are 'not verified for correctness'. The one reply found, by Adenwalla (9 Feb 2026), raises a congruence point about the construction for primes p ≤ k (L_j(n) ≡ Mn + b mod p). I did not establish whether it affects the argument. The conditional use of the open Schinzel's Hypothesis H is a limitation of scope, not a doubt about the implication.
events.direction: Cuts toward the affirmative answer, but only conditionally: it derives infinitude from Schinzel's Hypothesis H. It does not prove the unconditional question.
people: Abel (forum user; real identity and qualifications not established)

events.what_happened: A preprint on Cambridge Engage, dated 28 June 2026 per a search summary, claims a proof of infinitely many twin primes using a 'factorial-based primality criterion' the author calls 'Taha's Detector Prime Number'. The platform notes that it is not peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press. A reader comment rejects it. Not opened by me.
events.delivers: A claimed infinitude of twin primes, if valid. It does not bear on balanced primes: the Wikipedia article says that apart from 5, no member of a twin prime pair is balanced.
events.doubts: Platform says it is not peer-reviewed. A reader comment says the argument fails if one of the constructed numbers is not prime. I did not read the paper.
events.direction: Neither way for balanced primes. It is a claim about a neighbouring problem.

events.what_happened: Zenodo record 20758563: 'Fixed-Window Tower Sieve with Precision Period Cutting: A Proof of Polignac's Conjecture', version v12 published 24 June 2026 per a search result; earlier versions (v11, 19 June 2026, per a search summary) exist, and the first version is not established. Zenodo record 18369489 (version v1, 25 Jan 2026) claims an 'unconditional analytical closure' of Polignac's conjecture and is mainly numerical. Neither record opened by me.
events.revisions: Zenodo 20758563: v11 19 Jun 2026, v12 24 Jun 2026 (per search results). Zenodo 18369489: v1 25 Jan 2026. Earliest version not established.
events.delivers: A claimed proof, if valid, that every even number occurs as a prime gap infinitely often. This is a neighbouring problem and bears on balanced primes only indirectly, if at all.
events.time_since_posted: about 3.5 months for v12; the first version is not established
events.doubts: Self-published Zenodo records with several versions in a few weeks and no peer review. The January record is numerical evidence, which is not a proof. Not checked.
events.direction: Neither way for balanced primes. It concerns a different problem.

events.what_happened: OpenAI-hosted PDF 'Improved long gaps between primes' (cdn.openai.com, long_gaps.pdf). Per a search snippet and the Breakthrough Tracker record 'math-long-prime-gaps-iterated-log-bound-2026' (kingy.ai), it claims a lower bound on the largest prime gaps up to X that improves Rankin's classical bound by a factor log₂X. The tracker says the result is asymptotic with an unspecified positive constant, not an explicit new record gap. Per search summaries, the PDF credits GPT 6 Astra in its abstract and GPT 5.6 Sol in its introduction. Neither the PDF nor the tracker record was opened by me, and I could not fix the day of posting.
events.delivers: An asymptotic lower bound for maximal prime gaps, as summarised. It does not bear on balanced primes, whose condition is an equal-gap condition on three consecutive primes.
events.time_since_posted: about 2–3 months, date not pinned to the day
events.doubts: Unreviewed as of Aug 2026 per a search summary. A Magica report says an anonymous account filed a claim and that the public problem record labels it a partial proof. A Digg post says no verification or independent source appears in the packet. Both are secondary.
events.direction: Neither way for balanced primes. It is a neighbouring problem.

events.what_happened: Axiom Math announcement, 17 Aug 2026 per a search snippet: a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the 246 bounded-gap theorem (infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes differ by at most 246), produced by AxiomProver with 41 credited contributors (per the Breakthrough Tracker). A formalisation of an existing result, not a new bound. Not opened by me.
events.delivers: Formal verification of the existing bound H₁ ≤ 246. Not a new result, and not about balanced primes.
events.doubts: The Lean repository was not checked, so sorry-freeness is not established.
events.direction: Neither way for balanced primes. It is a formalisation of a neighbouring result.

events.what_happened: OpenAI preprint 'Improved Short Gaps Between Primes', dated 30 Aug 2026 and publicly announced 3 Sep 2026 (per the Breakthrough Tracker record, kingy.ai). It claims that infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes differ by at most 186, improving the published 246, by proving DHL[40,2]. The tracker attributes the work to 'GPT-6 Astra'. The tracker does not name human authors. I did not open the preprint, so no authors' own account of the system's role was obtained.
events.delivers: Infinitely many consecutive-prime gaps of at most 186, per the tracker. The Lean derivation is conditional on three explicit input axioms, including cited finite-field estimates and numerical bounds. Not about balanced primes.
events.remains: The whole balanced-prime problem. Also the twin-prime gap of 2, which the tracker says remains unproved.

machine_checked.system: Lean (per the tracker; repository not opened)

events.doubts: Tracker lists it as Peer reviewed: No and Provisional. It states that no independent human semantic review was located and that the numerical certificate does not discharge the three input axioms. Coverage conflicts on the model name (see disputes).
events.direction: Neither way for balanced primes. It is a bounded-gap result.

events.what_happened: Zhao Song and Song Yue (Northeastern University), 'Bounded Gaps Between Primes: An Upper Bound of 236', IACR ePrint 2026/1893. Received 4 Sep 2026, approved 9 Sep 2026. The abstract proves H₁ = liminf (p_{n+1} − p_n) ≤ 236. I read the abstract page. It does not mention balanced primes or consecutive primes in arithmetic progression.
events.delivers: H₁ ≤ 236: infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes with gap at most 236. The twin-prime gap H₁ = 2 is not reached. Not about balanced primes.
events.doubts: ePrint listing; no peer review shown on the page read. I did not read the full text.
events.direction: Neither way for balanced primes. It is a bounded-gap result.

disputes.summary: The conditional reduction of the k = 3 case to Schinzel's Hypothesis H is called 'folklore' by Abel, citing Schinzel–Sierpiński (1958) and Dubner et al. (2001). A reply on the earlier thread by Dogmachine attributes the same reduction to Schinzel–Sierpiński (1958). Neither attribution was checked against the source paper.

Sources name different models for the OpenAI prime-gap preprints. The Breakthrough Tracker credits the 186-bound preprint to 'GPT-6 Astra'; a news piece (search snippet) credits the same work to 'GPT-5.6 Sol'. For the large-gap PDF, a search summary says its abstract credits GPT 6 Astra and its introduction credits an earlier argument to GPT 5.6 Sol. I did not open the preprints to resolve this. Neither is about balanced primes.

summary: No source shows any unconditional progress on the infinitude of balanced primes between 26 Jan 2024 and 11 Oct 2026. The Erdős Problem #141 page (last edited 28 Sep 2025; accessed 11 Oct 2026) states that it is 'open, even for k=3, whether there are infinitely many such progressions'. The Wikipedia list (current, read in three chunks through a fetch summary) still carries 'Are there infinitely many balanced primes?' among the open problems. The Balanced prime article (fetch summary; last edited 1 Oct 2026) calls the infinitude a conjecture. The closest movement is conditional: an Aug 2025 forum sketch (Weisenberg) and a Feb 2026 forum post (Abel) reduce the k = 3 case, which is exactly the balanced-prime question, to Schinzel's Hypothesis H, which is itself open. I record it as a conditional implication, not progress, since the problem asks unconditionally. The competing reading is that a widely believed hypothesis plus a folklore label makes this conditionally settled; the record keeps that reading open for the judging pass. Neighbouring results are recorded as discounted events: Song–Yue bounded gaps H₁ ≤ 236 (Sep 2026); OpenAI's bounded gaps ≤ 186 preprint (30 Aug 2026, announced 3 Sep); Axiom's Lean formalisation of the 246 bound (Aug 2026); an OpenAI large-gap lower bound (2026); a June 2026 twin-prime claim; and Polignac claims on Zenodo. None concerns the balanced-prime condition. The Wikipedia article notes that apart from 5 no twin-prime member is balanced, so twin results do not transfer directly. Nothing I found names an AI system in connection with balanced primes. The Manifold market (about 95% Yes, a snapshot; its criterion is a 'well-accepted' proof) mentions no AI and is not evidence of a result. AI-term searches (queries 5, 14–16, 22, 23, 25, 26) found AI activity only on neighbouring problems: the OEIS Open benchmark (arXiv 2608.11941, which does not mention balanced primes or A006562 in the abstract page I read), Erdős problems, and the prime-gap preprints above. The OpenAI preprints and the Axiom formalisation are AI-related but neighbouring. For the Axiom formalisation, the system's role is formalisation of an existing proof, which DEEP_DIVE §5.4 does not count as the AI involvement sought. For the OpenAI preprints, the system is named only by the tracker and news, and I did not open the preprints, so no authors' own account was obtained. Under §5.4 I therefore list no system for them. Finite-instance facts: the largest known CPAP-3 is 15,004 digits (Batalov, Wikipedia as of 2023). A French Wikipedia mirror (2014) gives 10,546 digits for the largest balanced prime (Broadhurst); this conflicts with the English figure and is outdated, but it is finite data and moves nothing either way. Sources for the Wikipedia article, the Erdős page and the OEIS entry were read in full or in chunks through fetch summaries, so exact wording is paraphrase where I say so.
competing_reading: The conditional reduction (Abel, Feb 2026) is a short argument that makes the k = 3 case follow from Schinzel's Hypothesis H, which the field widely expects to be true. Together with the folklore label and a 95% Manifold market, one could say the question is settled conditionally on a widely accepted hypothesis and should be recorded as 'conditionally resolved', not open. Against this: the problem asks for an unconditional infinitude, the Erdős page (last edited Sep 2025) says the k = 3 case is open, and the argument rests on an open hypothesis, so the conditional result does not change the unconditional status.
what_would_settle_it: An unconditional proof, or a qualified expert's verification of one, that there are infinitely many three-term runs of consecutive primes in arithmetic progression. Alternatively, an update to the Erdős #141 status after Feb 2026, or a named expert's public assessment of the Abel reduction and of the Adenwalla remark. Full text of Eismann's arXiv:0711.0865 would settle the level (1;1) restatement. Opening the OpenAI preprints would settle which model, if any, was involved in the neighbouring results and what it did. Opening the OEIS Open 492-item list would settle whether any balanced-prime conjecture is in it.
